issues.legal_issue: Rights and obligations created under a temporary statute may survive its expiry when the statute and the nature of those rights and obligations show that they are enduring.
material_facts: Under a temporary statute, permission was granted to construct temporary structures subject to an express condition that they be removed when required to implement a town-planning scheme.
The statute provided that the benefit of permission would be annexed to and go with ownership of the structure.
After the statute expired, the competent authority directed the owner to remove the structures to give effect to the scheme.
issues.conclusion: The rights and obligations arising from the permission, including the authority’s right to enforce the removal condition, survived expiry of the temporary statute.
issues.legal_principle: Whether rights, restrictions, or obligations under a temporary statute survive its expiry depends on the statute’s construction and the nature and character of those rights and obligations; there is no inflexible rule that they lapse. Sections 3 and 8 of the City of Bombay (Building Works Restriction) Act, 1944, read with the express permission condition, made the removal obligation enduring and attached it to ownership. State of Orissa v. Bhupendra Kumar Bose was followed. The criminal-proceedings cases S. Krishnan v. State of Madras, State of Uttar Pradesh v. Seth Jagamander Das, and Gopi Chand v. Delhi Administration were distinguished; Steavenson v. Oliver and Warren v. Windle were referred to.

predicates.temporary_statute_permission_case: The case concerns rights or obligations arising from permission granted under a temporary statute.
predicates.permission_made_removal_condition_enduri: The permission expressly required the structure to be removed when called upon to give effect to a public improvement scheme.
predicates.removal_condition_attached_to_ownership: The statute made the benefit of the permission, and its associated conditions, attach to ownership of the structure.

issues.definition: When permission under a temporary statute imposes an enduring removal condition that attaches to ownership, the related rights and obligations survive the statute’s expiry.

issues.legal_issue: Expiry of a temporary statute supplemental to a permanent municipal statute does not terminate the statutory existence of the municipal functionary created under the permanent statute.
material_facts: The temporary statute was supplemental to the permanent municipal statute and referred to that statute as the principal statute.
The municipal commissioner was a functionary appointed under the permanent municipal statute.
After the temporary statute expired, the commissioner issued a notice enforcing a condition attached to construction permission.
issues.conclusion: The municipal commissioner did not cease to exist when the temporary statute expired and remained capable of exercising powers available under the applicable law.
issues.legal_principle: The temporary statute was supplemental to the Bombay Municipal Corporation Act, 1888. The commissioner was a functionary under that Act and was appointed from time to time under section 54; the commissioner’s existence therefore did not depend on the continued existence of the temporary statute.

predicates.commissioner_authority_case: The case concerns whether a municipal commissioner retained authority after expiry of a temporary statute.
predicates.temporary_statute_supplemented_permanent: The temporary statute supplemented a permanent municipal statute.
predicates.commissioner_office_created_by_permanent: The commissioner’s office and appointment derived from the permanent municipal statute.

issues.definition: When a temporary statute supplements permanent municipal law and the commissioner’s office derives from that permanent law, the commissioner continues to exist after the temporary statute expires.

issues.legal_issue: A demolition notice is not invalid merely because it cites an incorrect statutory source if the power to issue it is traceable to a valid source.
material_facts: A demolition notice identified the applicable town-planning scheme and stated that the land and temporary structure were affected by it.

The notice referred to a municipal provision as the source for carrying out demolition, but the notice was in substance issued under a special regulation incorporated into the town-planning legislation.
The special regulation supplied authority to require removal of temporary structures subject to a removal condition.
issues.conclusion: The notice was validly issued under the special regulation, and the mistaken reference to the municipal provision did not invalidate it.
issues.legal_principle: The notice was issued under Special Regulation 36, which became part of the Bombay Town Planning Act, 1954 under section 51(3). Regulations 36 and 38, section 55(1)(a), and Rule 28 made under section 87 supported enforcement. An incorrect citation does not vitiate an exercise of power when the power can be traced to a legitimate source. Afzal Ullah v. State of Uttar Pradesh, J.K. Steel Ltd. v. Union of India, N.B. Sanjana v. Elphinstone Mill, and H.L. Mehra v. Union of India were cited.

rule.if: demolition_notice_case and notice_identifies_applicable_scheme and valid_law_authorizes_demolition_notice and notice_cites_wrong_power

predicates.demolition_notice_case: The case concerns the validity of a notice directing removal or demolition of a structure.
predicates.notice_identifies_applicable_scheme: The notice identifies the public scheme affecting the land or structure.
predicates.valid_law_authorizes_demolition_notice: A valid legal source authorizes the authority to require removal or demolition in the circumstances.
predicates.notice_cites_wrong_power: The notice refers to an incorrect legal power despite being traceable to a valid source.

issues.definition: In a demolition-notice case, a notice identifying the applicable scheme remains valid despite an incorrect citation when valid law authorizes the notice.

issues.legal_issue: A competent authority’s statutory direction for demolition can constitute an order supporting a landlord’s eviction claim where the premises are required for the immediate purpose of carrying out that demolition.
material_facts: A landlord brought an eviction suit relying on the statutory ground concerning premises required for immediate demolition ordered by a local or competent authority.
The authority directed the owner to remove the temporary structure under statutory town-planning powers and an express condition of the construction permission.
The courts with special jurisdiction found that the premises were required for immediate demolition.
The direction disclosed the authority’s view that demolition was required for the town-planning scheme.
issues.conclusion: The demolition direction constituted an order within the meaning of the eviction ground, and the established requirement for immediate demolition supported eviction.
issues.legal_principle: Section 13(1)(hhh) of the Bombay Rents (Hotel and Lodging Houses Rates) Control Act, 1947 concerns compulsory demolition ordered by a local or competent authority, unlike clause (hh), which concerns a landlord’s own intention to demolish and rebuild. For clause (hhh), the order must be issued under the authority’s powers and disclose that, in its opinion, the premises are required for immediate demolition; the restrictions in section 13(3A) and sections 17A, 17B, and 17C do not apply. The statutory origin of the notice was supported by Special Regulations 36 and 38 and the town-planning legislation.

rule.if: eviction_proceeding_under_compulsory_demolition_ground and competent_authority_orders_demolition and order_discloses_immediate_demolition_need and lower_courts_find_immediate_need

predicates.eviction_proceeding_under_compulsory_dem: A landlord brings an eviction proceeding on the ground that a competent authority has ordered demolition required for an immediate purpose.
predicates.competent_authority_orders_demolition: A local or competent authority directs demolition under powers available to it.
predicates.order_discloses_immediate_demolition_nee: The direction discloses the authority’s view that the premises are required for immediate demolition.
predicates.lower_courts_find_immediate_need: The courts that determined the relevant facts find that the premises are required for immediate demolition.

issues.definition: In an eviction proceeding based on compulsory demolition, an authority’s demolition order supports eviction when it discloses an immediate need and the fact-finding courts find that need established.

issues.legal_issue: Partial suspension of a town-planning scheme and a proposed variation do not invalidate enforcement of regulations that remain in force or have not yet been varied.
material_facts: The government suspended certain regulations of the scheme but left the regulations governing removal of temporary structures and enforcement in force.
The scheme was not withdrawn or abandoned.
A proposed variation had not been brought into effect.
issues.conclusion: The partial suspension did not affect the notice because the relevant regulations remained operative, and the unimplemented proposal to vary the scheme had no legal consequence.
issues.legal_principle: Suspending some regulations is not equivalent to withdrawing or abandoning the scheme, particularly where the regulations relevant to the dispute remain in force. A proposed variation has no legal consequence before it is carried into effect. H.L. Mehra v. Union of India was referred to; Willow Wren Canal Carrying Co. Ltd. v. British Transport Commission was also cited concerning the legal effect of a proposal not yet enacted.

predicates.scheme_enforcement_case: The case concerns enforcement of a direction made to implement a town-planning scheme.
predicates.relevant_regulations_remain_in_force: The regulations material to the required enforcement remain in force despite suspension of other regulations.
predicates.proposed_variation_not_implemented: A proposed change to the scheme has not been brought into effect.

issues.definition: Enforcement remains available when the relevant scheme regulations continue in force and a proposed variation has not taken effect.

issues.legal_issue: A landlord may seek eviction on the ground of compulsory demolition even though the demolition direction was issued to the landlord rather than directly to the tenant.
material_facts: The authority directed the owner of the premises to remove the structure to implement the town-planning scheme.
The landlord sought eviction of the tenant on the statutory ground of premises required for immediate demolition ordered by a competent authority.
No material was produced to show that only the authority, and not the landlord, could evict the tenant on that ground.
The municipal statute allowed the landlord to obtain reasonable access to the leased premises to comply with the authority’s notice.
issues.conclusion: The landlord was not barred from seeking eviction; the tenant’s contention that only the local authority could evict was rejected.
issues.legal_principle: Section 13(1)(hhh) of the Bombay Rents (Hotel and Lodging Houses Rates) Control Act, 1947 provides the relevant eviction ground. Section 507 of the Bombay Municipal Corporation Act, 1888 allows a landlord to obtain an order requiring a tenant to provide reasonable facilities for entry so the landlord can comply with a municipal notice.

predicates.landlord_eviction_proceeding_under_compu: A landlord brings an eviction proceeding on the ground of premises required for compulsory demolition.
predicates.authority_directs_owner_to_remove_struct: A competent authority directs the owner to remove the structure.
predicates.landlord_must_comply_with_direction: The landlord must secure access to the premises or possession to comply with the authority’s direction.
predicates.no_law_shows_only_authority_can_evict: No applicable law or material establishes that only the authority, rather than the landlord, may evict the tenant on this ground.

issues.definition: A landlord may seek eviction for compulsory demolition when the authority directs the owner to remove the structure, the landlord must comply, and no rule reserves eviction exclusively to the authority.
